summary: Defines enhancements to OSPF to support Opaque LSAs, a new class of link-state advertisement that carries application-specific information through the network. It was replaced by RFC 5250.

eli5.summary: A way for routers to pass along extra notes inside their map-sharing messages, even if they do not understand them.

questions: what is an ospf opaque lsa
how to extend ospf with new information
subtitle: A general-purpose container that lets OSPF routers flood extra, application-specific data through the network.

tldr.problem: OSPF needed a generalized way to carry new kinds of information in its link-state database without defining a new advertisement type each time.
tldr.mechanism: Opaque LSAs are link-state types 9, 10 and 11: a standard LSA header followed by application-specific data, flooded with the normal OSPF mechanism but limited by a scope (link, area or whole AS) and sent only to neighbors that set the O-bit.
tldr.outcome: It was updated by RFC 3630 and replaced by RFC 5250.

facts.label: Opaque Type field
facts.value: first 8 bits of the link-state ID

today: RFC 2370 is obsolete. It was updated by RFC 3630 and replaced by RFC 5250.

sections.title: The Idea Behind Opaque LSAs
sections.content:
OSPF routers share link-state advertisements (LSAs) to build a common picture of the network. RFC 2370 defines a new class, the Opaque LSA, as a generalized mechanism for the future extensibility of OSPF. An Opaque LSA is a standard LSA header followed by a 32-bit aligned, application-specific information field.

The information may be used directly by OSPF or indirectly by some application that wants to distribute data through the OSPF domain. The RFC's own example is distributing IP to link-layer address resolution information. The exact use of Opaque LSAs is out of scope. An implementation is expected to offer an application interface to encapsulate and send or receive data, and to tell the application when previously received data may no longer be valid after a topology change.
sections.eli5: An opaque LSA is a labeled envelope the routers carry for someone else. The routers do not need to read the letter inside.

sections.title: The Opaque LSA Format
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are link-state types 9, 10 and 11. The usual LSA header is followed by Opaque Information, padded to 32-bit alignment.

The link-state ID is split in two: the first 8 bits are the Opaque Type and the remaining 24 bits are a type-specific Opaque ID. The LS type identifies the flooding scope.

  • Type 9: link-local; not flooded beyond the local (sub)network.
  • Type 10: area-local; not flooded beyond the borders of its area.
  • Type 11: flooded throughout the Autonomous System, with the same scope as AS-external (type-5) LSAs.
sections.eli5: The envelope has a stamp saying how far it may travel: just this street, just this town, or the whole country.

sections.title: Flooding Rules
sections.content:
Both sender and receiver are responsible for honoring the scope. A receiver must store a valid Opaque LSA but must not accept one that violates the scope.

  • Type 9 must not be flooded out an interface other than the one it was received on. Implementations should track the interface for each such LSA.
  • Type 10 must not be flooded out an interface in a different area than the one it arrived in.
  • Type 11 must not be flooded into a stub area. If one is received in a stub area it must be discarded and not acknowledged, because the neighbor flooded it in error.

Type-11 Opaque LSAs are flooded through all transit areas, not flooded into stub areas from the backbone, and not originated by routers into their stub areas.
sections.eli5: Each router checks the stamp on the envelope before passing it on, and refuses to send it farther than the stamp allows.

sections.title: Capability and Database Exchange
sections.content:
Optional OSPF advertisements are only flooded to routers that understand them. A router learns a neighbor is opaque-capable from the O-bit in the Options field of its Database Description packets while in state ExStart. A neighbor is opaque-capable if and only if it sets that bit, and Opaque LSAs are placed on a neighbor's retransmission list only if it is capable.

If a non-capable router does get one by accident, for example through a multicast Link State Update, it simply discards the LSA as an unknown LS type.

The only change to the neighbor state machine is the action for state ExStart, event NegotiationDone. The Database summary list now includes types 9 and 10 Opaque LSAs from the area, plus type-11 ones from the global structure. Type 11 is left out for virtual neighbors and stub areas, and type 9 is left out if the neighbor is on a different interface. LSAs at MaxAge go on the retransmission list instead.
sections.eli5: Routers first ask each other, "do you do envelopes?" Only those that say yes are sent any, so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two concerns apply to routing protocols: authenticating routing information, and denial of service from repeating the same advertisement or flooding the database with many distinct ones. The RFC says both exist whether or not a router supports the Opaque option.

OSPF's Cryptographic authentication option appends a message digest to packets; MD5 is currently the only algorithm specified. No standard OSPF authentication type provides confidentiality or protects against traffic analysis. Digital signatures are described in RFC 2154.

Repetition is limited by origination at most once every MinLSInterval (5 seconds) and acceptance at most once every MinLSArrival (1 second). Routers short of memory can be accommodated with stub areas and NSSAs.
sections.eli5: Routers must be sure a message is really from a friend, and must not be buried under endless copies of the same message. OSPF limits how often one can be sent.

sections.title: Opaque Type Allocation
sections.content: IANA maintains the Opaque types. A new type requires review by the OSPF working group, or a recommended Designated Expert if that group has disbanded. Values 0 to 127 are allocated by IETF Consensus action, and values 128 to 255 are reserved for private and experimental use.
sections.eli5: A central office hands out the envelope labels. Some are kept free for people to try their own ideas.
